Its high register is clear and translucent, with a pearly sheen, while the middle and low registers sound quiet and deep. The resonating body is pear-shaped and gives a warmth of its own, so the tone is neither as sharp as a guitar nor as airy as a harp. Where the pipa's plucked sound is drier and more forceful, the lute is softer and more finely shaded; beside keyboard instruments it keeps the warmth and expressiveness particular to strings. Its range is wide and its volume moderate but carrying; in a room it can sound intimate, and the resonance of its polyphonic chords shows many layers of sound.

Early lutes are already seen in Mesopotamia around 3100 BC; the short-necked almond-shaped body developed in Bactria and Gandhara and became the forerunner of the Islamic, Chinese, Japanese and European lute lines. In the Sasanian period it was called the barbat, which later became the oud. The Moors brought it to al-Andalus in 711, and in the eleventh century Iberian workshops influenced Provence and the rest of Europe. The European lute appears in documents of 1270, with five courses in the Middle Ages and a plectrum for accompaniment. At the end of the fifteenth century players took to the fingers and a sixth course was added, which allowed polyphony. From the fourteenth century it spread into the German-speaking lands, and around 1500 a family of makers worked in Füssen.

The lute is a plucked instrument, Hornbostel–Sachs number 321.321-5, and in the broad sense the term covers any necked string instrument whose strings run parallel to the soundboard; the European lute and the Near Eastern oud share an ancestor, and the guitar and the pipa belong to the lute family too. It is built with a neck joined to a hollow resonator with a deep rounded back, usually with a soundhole in the front, and it may be fretted or unfretted; the strings are tuned at the pegs, and the player plucks with one hand and stops the strings with the other to change the pitch. The European lute was used in many kinds of instrumental music from the Middle Ages to the Baroque; in the Renaissance it was an important instrument of secular music and accompanied vocal works and consorts, and in the Baroque it could take the basso continuo.
魯特琴琴身以木頭製成，音箱中空，正面有木質面板與音孔，背面呈突出圓弧，由木片高低: The body of the lute is made of wood: the resonator is hollow, the front has a wooden soundboard and a soundhole, and the back is a bulging curve built of staves set edge to edge like ribs. The neck uses a light wood and the fingerboard a harder, thicker board; the material of the pegbox is not recorded. The strings are generally gut; in the early seventeenth century bass strings were sometimes made of lead or other metal, in the middle of that century they became a gut core wound with fine metal wire, and modern players also use nylon and other synthetic fibres. The medieval European lute was played with a feather plectrum, and the traditional oud with a wooden one.
